source_refs.note: Topic 16.8 with Figs. 16.11-16.13 and Example 16.9 (PDF 76-77, printed 16-17), as printed.

blocks.text: Many electric circuits consist of both capacitors and resistors. Fig.16.11 shows a resistor-capacitor circuit called R-C-circuit. When the switch S is set at terminal A, the R-C combination is connected to a battery of voltage V₀ which starts charging the capacitor through the resistor R.

blocks.alt: A circuit with a resistor R and a capacitor C (plates +q and -q) in the top wire. On the right a switch S is set to terminal A, which puts the battery Vo (bottom wire) in the loop; terminal B is on a wire leading back to the left side. A loop of arrows shows the charging current going clockwise.
blocks.caption: Figure 16.11: R-C circuit with switch S at A (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.11).

blocks.alt: Graph of charge q against time t for a charging capacitor. Two curves rise from zero towards the dashed level CVo = qo, one quickly (small RC) and one slowly (large RC). A dashed level 0.63qo meets each curve; dashed lines drop to the time axis, where RC is marked for each curve.
blocks.caption: Figure 16.12: Growth of charge with time for a small and a large time constant RC (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.12).

blocks.text: The capacitor is not charged immediately, rather charges build up gradually to the equilibrium value of q₀ = CV₀. The growth of charge with time for different resistances is shown in Fig.16.12. According to this graph q = 0 at t = 0 and increases gradually with time till it reaches its equilibrium value q₀ = CV₀. The voltage V across capacitor at any instant can be obtained by dividing q by C, as V = q/C.

How fast or how slow the capacitor is charging or discharging, depends upon the product of the resistance R and the capacitance C used in the circuit. As the unit of product RC is that of time, so this product is known as time constant and is defined as the time required by the capacitor to deposit 0.63 times the equilibrium charge q₀. The graphs of Fig.16.12 show that the charge reaches its equilibrium value sooner when the time constant is small.

Fig.16.13 (a) illustrates the discharging of a capacitor through a resistor. In this figure, the switch S is set at point B, so the charge +q on the left plate can flow anti-clockwise through the resistance and neutralize the charge -q on the right plate.

blocks.alt: Two parts. (a) The same R-C circuit with the switch S set to B, so the battery is left out; a loop of arrows shows the current flowing anticlockwise from the +q plate through R to the -q plate. (b) Graph of q against t: two curves start at CVo and fall towards zero, quickly for small RC and slowly for large RC.
blocks.caption: Figure 16.13: (a) Discharging a capacitor through a resistor with S at B; (b) charge against time for small and large RC (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.13).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 16.13(a) draws the arrow on the top of the current loop pointing the opposite way to the arrows on the left and bottom, so the printed arrows disagree. The text says the charge +q flows anti-clockwise through the resistance to the −q plate; the drawing above follows the text and shows all arrows anti-clockwise.
The graphs in Fig.16.13 (b) shows that discharging begins at t = 0 when q = CV₀ and decreases gradually to zero. Smaller values of time constant RC lead to a more rapid discharge.

blocks.title: Example 16.9
blocks.problem: The time constant of a series RC circuit is τ = RC. Verify that an ohm times farad is equivalent to second.
steps:
Ohm's law in terms of potential difference V, current I and resistance R can be written as,
V = IR

Putting I = q/t, this equation transforms into the equation,
V = (q/t)R or R = (V × t)/q
According to equation q = CV, C = q/V

Multiplying this equation with above equation gives,
RC = (V × t)/q × q/V = τ

Hence 1 ohm × 1 farad = 1 second
Where ohm is the unit of resistance R.
